By Charumini de Silva

The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce last week launched the Sri Lanka–Vietnam Business Council, seeking to give fresh institutional momentum to bilateral trade, investment and tourism ties at a time when political and diplomatic relations between the two countries are gaining strength, though the commercial exchanges remain below their potential.

The new council, the 22nd bilateral business council established under the Ceylon Chamber, has attracted 30 inaugural members, signalling growing private-sector interest in Vietnam and the opportunities emerging from closer economic relations.

Council formed amid push to deepen commercial ties

The launch follows commitments made during Vietnamese Party General Secretary and State President Tô Lâm’s State visit to Sri Lanka in May, when a Sri Lanka–Vietnam Trade, Investment and Tourism Forum brought together government and business representatives from both countries.

Ceylon Chamber Chairperson Krishan Balendra said the new council was intended to move those discussions from dialogue to sustained commercial engagement.

“This is an important milestone in the growing economic partnership between our two countries,” he said, describing the council as a platform to facilitate business partnerships, promote bilateral trade and investment, encourage knowledge sharing and strengthen private sector engagement.

“As we launch the business council today, I am confident that it will serve as a catalyst of stronger partnerships, increased trade and investments, and deeper collaboration between the private sectors of Sri Lanka and Vietnam,” he added.

Trade remains below $ 500m as $ 1 b target looms

The urgency of strengthening the commercial relationship was underscored by Vietnamese Ambassador to Sri Lanka Trinh Tam, who noted that bilateral trade has yet to cross the $ 500 million mark in any recent year.

This is despite the two countries having maintained diplomatic relations for more than 55 years and having recently elevated their relationship to a Comprehensive Partnership.

“Our economic, trade and investment cooperation is still under expectation,” she said, noting that the two countries’ leaders have nevertheless set an ambitious $ 1 billion bilateral trade target by 2030.

She said stronger Government-to-Government (G2G) relations alone would not be sufficient to achieve that ambition. “For this partnership to grow further, we need not only close G2G relations, but also stronger connections between our businesses and our people.”

The Ambassador said the new Business Council could provide the practical mechanism for companies to meet, exchange market information, identify opportunities and develop partnerships.

Vietnam’s growth opens opportunities for Sri Lankan businesses

Balendra highlighted Vietnam’s rapid economic transformation and its emergence as a major manufacturing, logistics and investment hub in Asia as key reasons for Sri Lankan companies to engage more actively with the market.

He identified manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, tourism, ICT, renewable energy and professional services as areas with potential for greater cooperation.

“Sri Lanka’s strategic location in the Indian Ocean, strong services sector and growing tourism potential offer Vietnamese companies with opportunities for partnerships and regional access,” he outlined. 

He said the Chamber’s earlier ‘Doing Business in Vietnam’ event in October 2025 had already generated considerable interest among Sri Lankan businesses. “It showed a strong appetite for exploring opportunities in one of Asia's fastest-growing economies,” Balendra said.

The council, he added, would provide a structured platform to identify new opportunities and address common challenges rather than functioning simply as another business association.

“We warmly invite interested companies and stakeholders to become part of this initiative and join us in shaping the next chapter of Sri Lanka-Vietnam economic relations,” Balendra said.

Direct flights begin translating into business links

Improved connectivity is emerging as one of the most immediate enablers of the relationship.

Balendra also highlighted that the expansion of services by Vietnam Airlines and Vietjet had significantly improved connectivity between the two countries, making travel easier for businesses, investors and tourists.

The Ambassador pointed out that the direct flights had already begun producing tangible business interest. She said since Vietnam Airlines and Vietjet Air commenced direct services between Ho Chi Minh City and Colombo around two months ago, the Vietnamese Embassy has facilitated about 10 groups of Vietnamese businessmen visiting Sri Lanka to explore the market and promote their products.

“Though still small in size, they are positive signals for incoming business connections between Vietnam and Sri Lanka,” she said.

The development could therefore become more than a tourism catalyst, with direct connectivity helping reduce one of the practical barriers to business-to-business engagement.

Focus urged on SMEs and new areas

She also urged the new Council to ensure that the relationship does not become concentrated solely among large corporations.

The Ambassador called for greater participation by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), young entrepreneurs and businesses operating in emerging areas, arguing that the council should help move discussions beyond potential opportunities towards actual projects.

“Most importantly, turn ideas into real projects,” she stressed, outlining the Council’s role in connecting companies, sharing information and facilitating partnerships.

The Ambassador also outlined trade, investment, tourism, logistics, agriculture, food products and services as areas offering particularly strong potential.

From friendship to tangible economic gains

Addressing the gathering as the Council’s first President, Mahen Kariyawasan stressed the need to transform the two countries’ longstanding friendship into measurable economic outcomes.

“I believe our two countries have tremendous potential to complement each other's strengths and expand our economic engagement. While our diplomatic and cultural relations are strong, there is considerable scope to further develop our trade, investment and tourism partnerships,” he added.

Noting that Sri Lanka and Vietnam already had a strong foundation built on historical ties, cultural understanding and people-to-people relations; Kariyawasan said the challenge was to convert that goodwill into commercial outcomes.

“Our objective must be to transform the longstanding friendship between our two nations into tangible economic benefits. We must actively encourage business-to-business partnerships, organise trade delegations, promote investment opportunities and create a platform where entrepreneurs from both countries can work together,” he added.

He identified tourism, aviation, agriculture, manufacturing, technology and logistics as priority areas and called for business-to-business partnerships, trade delegations and investment promotion to be placed at the centre of the council’s work.

Kariyawasan insisted on an inclusive platform that would allow SMEs to participate alongside larger companies. “I also believe that this Council must be inclusive, providing opportunities not only for large corporations but also for SMEs to participate in and benefit from our growing relationship,” he said.

A platform to shape next phase

The formation of the Sri Lanka-Vietnam Business Council comes as both countries seek to give greater economic substance to an increasingly close diplomatic relationship.

“As we inaugurate this Council, let us remember that we are not merely establishing another business organisation. We are creating a bridge between two friendly nations, with the potential to generate new opportunities, strengthen commercial ties and contribute to the prosperity of our people. I look forward to working closely with the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, both Embassies, our respective governments and the private sectors of our two countries to make this Council a truly successful and dynamic institution,” Kariyawasan said.

Balendra said the combination of institutional engagement, growing business interest and enhanced air connectivity provided a promising foundation. “We warmly invite interested companies and stakeholders to become part of this initiative and join us in shaping the next chapter of bilateral economic relations. The future of Sri Lanka-Vietnam economic relations is both promising and exciting,” he added.

The inaugural Sri Lanka-Vietnam Business Council Executive Committee Members comprise; Senior Vice President Sanjaya Rajaguru (Millennium Transportation-Director), Vice President Kamal Wimalaratne (Hayleys Engineering Ltd.,-Director and CEO), Treasurer Malith Thilakarathne (Nations Trust Bank-Deputy Manager), Dilush Perera (Hirdaramani-Finance Director), Ravi Jayawardena (Maliban-Group CEO), Sajeewa Ranasinghe (Agstar PLC-CEO), Chandana Jirasingha (Aitken Spence Cargo-Director) and Naveen Goonawardena (Linea Aqua Ltd.,-Senior Business Analyst).

The Sri Lanka Apparel Exporters Association (SLAEA) and Stredge Consulting Middle East successfully co-hosted ‘Traceability in Practice: From Customer Expectations to Factory Reality,’ a virtual webinar and panel discussion recently. The session drew live participation from attendees in Sri Lanka including representatives from Stredge Sri Lanka and over ten other countries, including the UAE, France, England, India, Pakistan, Canada and Jordan, underscoring the international relevance of the issue to Sri Lanka’s apparel and textile export sector.

The webinar addressed one of the most pressing challenges faced by the local exporters today: how evolving European Union regulations on sustainability, ESG reporting and product traceability including the EU’s forthcoming Digital Product Passport, are pushing requirements deeper into global supply chains, often well beyond a factory’s direct, Tier 1 suppliers.

“Sri Lanka’s apparel industry has repeatedly turned changing global expectations into competitive strength, from ethical manufacturing to green manufacturing. Traceability is the next chapter in that story, and one this industry is well placed to lead,” remarked SLAEA Chairperson Rajitha Jayasuriya. 

The event’s centerpiece was a 35-minute industry panel featuring; MAS Holdings Manager-Supply Chain Strategy and Development Navindu Munidasa, Noyon Lanka CEO Husni Salieh and Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) Secretary General Yohan Lawrence moderated by Stredge Consulting Middle East CEO and Partner Chester Cruse. The panel enabled insights into ground-level practical barriers Sri Lankan exporters’ face in tracing garments and raw materials beyond their immediate suppliers.

Stredge Consulting Middle East’s Prasanna Hettiarachchi framed the industry-wide shift as one of governance and opportunity. “This isn’t the first time the apparel industry had braved challenges.  We’ve overcome them before and made them into a competitive advantage and we need to do the same again,” noted Hettiarachchi who maintained that Compliance is the mechanism and market access is the objective.

The program also brought an international dimension to the discussion. Julien Bonne of Bureau Veritas, a world leader in testing, inspection, and certification services, helping clients meet the growing challenges of quality, safety, environmental protection, and social responsibility, shared a European buyer’s perspective on what brands will expect from apparel supply chains under incoming market-access rules, while Alex Lheritier, Chairman of Koaloo.FI, a France-based fintech that turns supply chain risk into immediate profit for international corporates, suppliers, and banks and has earned awards such as the ESG Fintech 100 and the WTO’s Best AI Solution for SMEs, addressed the technology and financing solutions that can enable trust and transparency across the supply chain. 

Noting that the session is a strong first step toward an ongoing industry conversation, Stredge Consulting Middle East’s CEO and Partner Cruse averred: “This is a conversation the whole industry needs to be part of, exporters, financiers, technology providers and policymakers alike. We look forward to building on today’s discussion with further collaboration between SLAEA, Stredge and the wider apparel ecosystem.”

The meeting also considered opportunities to promote Sri Lankan tea, cinnamon, spices, gems and jewellery, agricultural products, rubber and coconut-based products, apparel and ICT services among New Zealand importers. Tourism, education, sports, student exchanges and improved air connectivity were discussed as further avenues for strengthening commercial and people-to-people relations.

The parties expressed their interest in continuing engagement to translate the FCCISL-developed Strategic Cooperation Plan into practical initiatives through an appropriate policy framework and coordinated institutional arrangements. Indian life sciences group Zydus Lifesciences Ltd., and Sri Lanka’s Sunshine Holdings PLC are partnering to invest over $ 20 million in a pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Horana, in a move aimed at expanding local medicine production and reducing reliance on imports.

The proposed joint venture, Zydus Sunshine Lifesciences Ltd., signed an agreement with the Board of Investment of Sri Lanka (BOI) to establish the facility within the BOI zone in Horana. The project will be developed on a site of nearly four acres, with commercial operations targeted for 2028, subject to project timelines and regulatory approvals.

The investment brings together Zydus’ international pharmaceutical manufacturing expertise and Sunshine Healthcare’s established presence in Sri Lanka’s healthcare market, with the initial phase focused on producing oral solid dosage medicines for domestic consumption.

Local production is expected to strengthen the country’s pharmaceutical manufacturing base, improve medicine supply-chain resilience and support access to quality medicines. The investment also comes amid continued efforts to reduce Sri Lanka’s dependence on imported pharmaceuticals and build domestic capacity in essential healthcare products.

Beyond manufacturing capacity, the venture is expected to facilitate technology transfer and develop local expertise in pharmaceutical production, quality assurance, and scientific and technical functions.

More than 80% of the facility’s workforce is expected to comprise Sri Lankan nationals, with specialised training and capability development planned to build skills in the high-value pharmaceutical industry.

Zydus Lifesciences operates across pharmaceuticals and consumer wellness, with an emerging medical technology business and an international presence spanning the United States, India and other markets. The group employs around 30,000 people worldwide, including 1,500 scientists engaged in research and development.

Sunshine Healthcare, the healthcare arm of Sunshine Holdings PLC, has operations spanning pharmaceuticals, medical devices, retail, manufacturing, research and development, and distribution. Its local market presence is expected to support the joint venture’s access to Sri Lanka’s healthcare sector.

The Horana facility will add to the BOI’s portfolio of manufacturing investments, with the venture seeking to combine international expertise with domestic production and workforce development.

The project’s contribution to import substitution and medicine security will depend on its eventual production capacity, product range and ability to meet domestic demand once commercial operations begin.

title: TISL calls for withdrawal of new anti-terror Bill | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 16 October 2026 00:02

Transparency International Sri Lanka (TISL) has called on the Government to withdraw the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill. The organisation warned that the Bill threatens fundamental rights, judicial independence and democratic freedoms.

The Bill, Gazetted on 22 September, 2026, seeks to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). TISL also urged the Government to repeal the PTA without further delay.

TISL said the Bill defines terrorism so broadly that it extends to damage to property, the environment, cultural property and electronic systems. This risks bringing offences better dealt with under ordinary criminal law within the scope of counter-terrorism legislation. Such sweeping definitions could also lead to disproportionate restrictions on freedom of expression and association, and on legitimate civic activity, it said.

The organisation also flagged provisions granting the armed forces and the Coast Guard extensive powers of arrest, search, seizure and questioning. Without adequate safeguards, it said, these powers could create accountability gaps and raise the risk of arbitrary action.

On detention, TISL noted that the Bill allows the Secretary to the Ministry of Defence to issue detention orders for an initial period of two months, while limiting a Magistrate’s ability to independently assess whether detention is necessary. It warned that this would concentrate excessive power in the executive and weaken judicial oversight.

TISL raised similar concerns over provisions allowing the President to proscribe organisations without specified time limits or adequate safeguards. It said this could lead to arbitrary restrictions on freedom of association and civic activity.

While acknowledging the State’s responsibility to address legitimate national security concerns, TISL said counter-terrorism legislation must not undermine fundamental rights, due process or judicial independence. It called for any replacement law to set clear limits on executive authority, establish effective accountability mechanisms and include adequate safeguards against arbitrary detention and the misuse of counter-terrorism powers.

The Court of Appeal has dismissed an appeal by a Buddhist monk convicted of sexually abusing a novice monk. The court upheld his conviction and sentences of 10 years’ rigorous imprisonment for grave sexual abuse.

Court of Appeal Justices Amal Ranaraja and Dr. Sumudu Premachandra held that the trial judge was entitled to rely on the child victim’s evidence, having found it credible and trustworthy. The bench said the victim had given a detailed and consistent account. The contradiction identified during cross-examination, it found, did not relate to the central allegations of sexual abuse.

The Polonnaruwa High Court had convicted the monk on two counts of grave sexual abuse under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. The offences occurred between 23 November, 2014 and 23 January, 2015, when the victim was seven years old and living at the same temple as the accused, a senior monk.

The High Court imposed 10 years’ rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 50,000 on each count, with six months’ simple imprisonment in default of each fine. The prison terms were ordered to run concurrently. The accused was also ordered to pay Rs. 100,000 in compensation to the victim.

Additional Solicitor General Shanil Kularatne appeared for the Attorney General.

title: Growth paradox – Numbers vs. benefits: Part I – Reforming public sector | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 16 October 2026 00:26
-     - 45

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has identified a gap between Government objectives and its implementation arm (File pic)

Introduction

After reading my previous article, “What Produces Economic Growth — and What Does Economic Growth Produce?”, my friend Pali sent me this message: “Chandre. In your next article, can you outline what we should do about these paradoxes of ‘growth’?”

I agreed. But only after starting this piece did, I realise what Pali meant by his diplomatic language: “Buddy, being constructive is not as easy as being critical.”

In my previous article, I presented six numbers:

These numbers illustrate the paradox. The economy is growing, but the benefits of growth are not reaching all households equally. What we should do to ensure growth benefits are widely and fairly shared?

The NPP philosophy

The NPP election manifesto, A Thriving Nation – A Beautiful Life, ends its preface with: “It is our goal to involve all communities in the process—from designing a production economy to ensuring fair distribution of its benefits.”

Presenting the Policy Statement at the inauguration of the Tenth Parliament on 23 November 2024, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said that the growth model would reflect “a production-oriented, regionally balanced economy.” His maiden Budget speech in 2025 carried the same philosophy: “Growth for the sake of growth has little value to society unless it is a means to uplifting the lives of all members of society.”

He further stated that growth should be inclusive, providing enhanced economic opportunities and ensuring that its benefits are fairly shared among all strata of society.

These statements reiterate the paradox of growth. Question is who and how translates the Government philosophy into action to address the paradox?

Gap between objectives and implementation

However noble the intentions, their realisation depends on implementation, follow-up and monitoring. That responsibility rests largely with the public service—the implementation arm of Government.

The President has identified a gap between Government objectives and its implementation arm. In his Policy Statement, he observed: “No matter how ambitious the goals and expectations of political leaders may be, those goals can only be realised if there is a well-structured and responsive public service to implement them.”

Addressing the District Secretaries and Divisional Secretaries Conference in December 2024, he said the public service had deviated from its intended objectives and required significant reforms to restore its effectiveness.

At the Economic Summit organised by the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce in February 2025, he also pledged to introduce policies, regulations, rules, procedures and processes to drastically shorten the time taken to get things done.

What the President states is: Ambitious policies require an implementation machinery capable of delivering them.

Is the public sector not capable of delivering?

Public perception of the public service is not very different from President’s view. It is often criticised as too large, bureaucratic, over-regulated, inefficient, indecisive and insufficiently responsive. There is also a perception that imagination, creativity and forward thinking have little room in the system. Every criticism may not be justified. But the message in it cannot be ignored.

The origins of our present public service go back to the nineteenth century. A centralised civil service was established under British rule in 1833. It was abolished in 1963 and replaced by the Ceylon Administrative Service, renamed the Sri Lanka Administrative Service in 1972.

Public Service was designed to fulfill the needs of a different country and a different era. Since then, the public sector has expanded enormously in size, layers, responsibilities, functions and workload. Yet much of its institutional framework continues to operate under old Acts, Ordinances, Regulations and practices.

Is the problem with the people or with the system?

The problem is not simply with the people working in the system. It may be the system itself. Hierarchy is deeply embedded in public-sector culture and leaves little room for teamwork and coordination.

I was once told an interesting story by the late Ken Balendran when he was Chairman of the Bank of Ceylon. His office was on the topmost floor of the bank’s headquarters, popularly known as “Pittu Bambuwa”, then the tallest building in Colombo. One day he walked down to the floor below to discuss something with the General Manager. When he returned, his personal assistant rushed in, surprised. “Sir, why did you walk down to the GM’s office? It never happens. If you want to discuss something with the GM, you can summon him to your office.”

That small incident illustrates the hierarchy built in to the system. The problem, however, goes beyond the hierarchy. The public sector has accumulated a set of ready-made explanations for delays and shortfalls—bad weather, elections, pandemics, delays in funds, conflicts in the Middle East or somewhere else. Officials are busy in chasing events rather than outcomes.

Tasks are often vertically assigned to individuals, units or divisions without assigning clear targets. The system is more concerned with following rules than achieving results.

The public sector is famously bound by AR and FR. Later came JR, followed by GR. More recently, there is ACR—Anti-Corruption Regulations.

All these rules have legitimate purposes. But when rules multiply without corresponding flexibility, discretion begins to look like an offence.

When I joined the public service as a clerk in 1964, the first document I received was a duty list. I continued issuing duty lists throughout my career until retirement. This raises the question: Is the public sector managing duties, or managing results?

With an ailing implementation machinery, no Government can overcome the paradoxes of growth.

The first step, therefore, should be to repair and revitalise the implementation machinery.

Towards a people-centric public service

The paradoxes of growth cannot be resolved merely by producing a higher GDP growth rate. Growth must translate into benefits: jobs, incomes, productivity, investment, regional development, better services and improved household welfare. Sri Lanka wants a production-oriented, regionally balanced and inclusive economy. For that, policies must be implemented effectively. The implementation machinery of Government must be capable of delivering. Public-sector reform is not merely an administrative issue. It is an economic-growth issue.

Sri Lanka needs a well-structured, responsive, competent, coordinated and people-centric public service. State delivers its promises to the citizen through the public service machinery.

1. From silos to systems

Government agencies often prepare annual plans around budgetary allocations and immediate issues. Agriculture provides a good example. During cultivation, attention is given to seeds, planting material, fertiliser and other inputs. At harvest time, attention shifts to disposal and marketing of the product. But agriculture is a value chain—covering production, inputs, finance, technology, storage, transport, processing, marketing and exports. Different agencies are involved in each stage. Responsibility goes beyond Ministry of Agriculture.

What is required is a holistic, coordinated and needs-based approach that considers the entire value chain rather than its fragmented components. The public service must move from silos to systems. Public agencies should work with the private sector, chambers, universities and other stakeholders. Regular monitoring should be in place to identify not only delays but also their causes and the remedial action required.

Responsibility for major tasks should be assigned to teams rather than individuals, with clear targets and Key Performance Indicators. Teams should report periodically on what has been completed, what is delayed, the difficulties encountered and proposed solutions.

This requires performance-based systems, simplified approvals, simpler documentation, digital platforms and mechanisms for inter-agency coordination.

2. Revisit outdated laws and regulations

The role and responsibilities of the public sector have changed dramatically, but many institutions still operate under legislation designed for another era.

Examples include the Railways Ordinance of 1902, Forest Conservation Ordinance of 1907 and Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance of 1937. Other major legislation dates from the 1970s, while free education itself was introduced in the 1940s.

Old legislation is not necessarily bad. The question is whether it remains fit for purpose. Sri Lanka’s economic, technological, social and international environment has changed profoundly. Its public sector cannot move forward along with these changes siting on obsolete acts and ordinances.

A genuine transformation therefore requires a systematic review of Acts, Ordinances and Regulations and their modernisation where necessary.

3. Simplify procedures

Complicated time-consuming procedures are a major source of delay in areas such as foreign investment, exports, taxation, local investment and SME participation. The burden falls particularly heavily on ordinary citizens and small businesses that lack lawyers, accountants and administrative staff to navigate complex systems.

Complexity has become a barrier. It can create opportunities for excessive bureaucracy, delays, bribery and corruption. The answer is Keep things simple. Procedures, approvals and documentation should be simplified wherever possible to reduce cost, delay, stress and inconvenience while improving productivity and fast-tracking decision-making.

4. Decentralise services

Many public services remain heavily centralised in and around Colombo, including obtaining identity cards, passports, driving licences, EPF/ETF benefits and pensions. This imposes unnecessary travel, cost and inconvenience on citizens while contributing to congestion, pollution and fuel consumption.

Until digitalisation is fully operational, functions that can reasonably be decentralised should be handled closer to citizens. For example, receiving applications, checking documents and making recommendations could, where appropriate, be undertaken through District Secretariats. This would move the Government closer to the citizen instead of citizens move towards Government.

From title to action

Over the years titles of public servants have changed. A General was added to titles of Directors, Commissioners, and Controllers. Peon is a KKS; Clerk is a Management Assistant; Watcher is a security officer. Whether the outlook, attitude and efficiency have changed along with titles is questionable. The public service attracts the cream of the education and people of considerable calibre, competence and capacity. Whether an environment is created to capitalise on that capacity is questionable.

Public servants need a framework with clear objectives, guidance and the freedom to deliver. Today, seniority matters. What should matter is the performance. Specific tasks should be assigned with clear time targets, and performance tracked against them. A public servant should know: What am I expected to deliver? By when? How will my success be measured? Is my performance recognised?

The objective should be to create a culture in which achievement attracts recognition and responsibility produces results and accountability. That would strengthen commitment, improve delivery and restore public confidence.

Conclusion

This is only the first step of a long journey to explain what we should do about paradoxes of ‘growth’. I have offered these ideas partly from my experience in the public service and partly from what I believe is required to address the present challenges. I would not have covered the turf well. There can be many gaps. I wanted to intrigue a dialogue with the objective of creating a public service with public servants not by title, but in action to revitalise the implementation machinery.

Continued with part II to suggest other steps.

Inauguration of the Sri Lanka Economic Summit

Labour reform is emerging as a critical priority in Sri Lanka’s efforts to attract the next wave of foreign direct investment (FDI) and accelerate economic growth. Speakers at the recent economic summit highlighted the need to address labour market constraints, skills shortages and workforce productivity. As Govindasamy noted, Sri Lanka faces challenges in remaining competitive with several regional neighbours on labour costs and productivity. Although labour reform has been discussed for decades, the need for decisive action has become increasingly urgent.

Sri Lanka’s ability to attract investment, expand high-value industries and create sustainable employment will depend significantly on its capacity to develop a skilled, productive and future-ready workforce, supported by flexible labour laws that facilitate job creation, business growth and responsible restructuring.

Crucially, this is also about retaining our young people. Sri Lanka cannot afford to educate and train its next generation only to see them leave because they cannot find productive jobs, competitive wages or credible career opportunities at home.

Bridging the skills gap

One of Sri Lanka’s persistent challenges is the mismatch between the skills people acquire and those employers require. Sectors such as construction, tourism, manufacturing, healthcare and technology need workers with relevant technical, professional and practical competencies. Yet many young people struggle to find suitable employment, while businesses report difficulties recruiting qualified staff.

This is not simply an education problem; it is a coordination challenge involving schools, universities, vocational training institutions, employers and policymakers.

Education and training must respond more directly to labour market demand. Employers should help identify emerging skills requirements, shape curricula, offer apprenticeships and provide workplace exposure. Training institutions must be accountable for graduate employability, rather than focusing primarily on enrolment and certification.

A national vision towards 2030

Sri Lanka needs a clear national vision for labour towards 2030, supported by effective leadership, realistic targets, adequate funding and stronger coordination between Government institutions and the private sector. An integrated national workforce strategy should connect education, vocational training, employment, migration and economic development.

Effective Cabinet-level leadership is essential to establish priorities, implementation timelines and transparent accountability. A reliable labour market information system would help identify occupational shortages, anticipate future demand and align training investments with industries offering the greatest potential for productive employment.

Building a future-ready workforce

Digitalisation, artificial intelligence, automation and changing global supply chains are transforming the nature of work. Sri Lanka must prepare its workforce for these changes through technical education, digital competencies, problem-solving skills and lifelong learning.

Greater private sector participation is indispensable. Businesses should invest in employee development, work-based learning and partnerships with educational institutions. Vocational and post-secondary education must become more accessible and relevant to emerging employment opportunities.

We must also unlock the potential of underutilised talent by addressing barriers to workforce participation, including through better career guidance, childcare support, flexible working arrangements and opportunities for reskilling.

Labour reform as an investment imperative

For investors, labour availability is not simply a question of numbers. They need access to workers with the right skills, at competitive costs, supported by reliable training systems and a regulatory environment that enables enterprises to grow. Labour laws should provide sufficient flexibility for businesses to adapt to changing market conditions, expand operations and restructure responsibly, while safeguarding workers’ rights and fair treatment.

A predictable and balanced labour framework can strengthen investor confidence. Combined with improved productivity, it can help Sri Lanka attract new investment, expand existing businesses and move into higher-value industries.

Creating jobs and retaining our young people

The ultimate test of labour reform is whether it creates more productive employment and improves living standards. Young Sri Lankans need opportunities to build careers, earn competitive incomes and progress professionally without feeling that leaving the country is their only route to success.

Attracting FDI must therefore go hand in hand with developing local talent. Investors should be encouraged to create skilled jobs, transfer knowledge, strengthen management capabilities and establish training partnerships with local institutions. Employers, too, must recognise that attracting and retaining talent requires competitive remuneration, good working conditions and credible career development.

Where genuine labour shortages persist, managed foreign recruitment may be necessary in selected sectors. However, this should complement, not replace, efforts to develop the domestic workforce and bring more people into productive employment.

Sri Lanka’s next wave of FDI will depend not only on the opportunities it offers investors, but also on the quality, productivity and adaptability of its workforce. Labour reform is not merely about making it easier to do business; it is about making it possible for Sri Lankans, particularly our young people, to build productive and rewarding lives in their own country.

The time has come to move from discussion to implementation. A clear national labour strategy towards 2030, backed by coordinated leadership and sustained public-private collaboration, can help strengthen competitiveness, attract investment and create the employment opportunities Sri Lanka needs for its next phase of growth.

title: Lanka’s renewable energy future: Are we solving real problems or undermining our own success? | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 16 October 2026 00:24
-     - 43

During the Q&A with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Economic and Investment Summit, moderator and Vice Chairperson Bingumal Thewarathanthri raised two important questions, one of which concerned the proposed change in the feed-in tariff methodology.

In his response, he spoke extensively about expanding the transmission network. However, he failed to address an equally important, if not more critical, issue: the modernisation and expansion of the distribution network, which is the backbone of distributed renewable energy generation.

This distinction is fundamental to understanding the real challenges facing Sri Lanka's renewable energy sector.

1. Rooftop solar has reduced electricity costs, not increased them

Of approximately 3,000 MW of installed solar capacity in Sri Lanka, more than 2,550 MW has reportedly been developed through the feed-in tariff framework, predominantly through rooftop solar installations.

This renewable energy capacity has contributed to displacing more expensive electricity generation, with an estimated avoided generation cost exceeding Rs. 22 per unit.

Yet rooftop solar has increasingly been portrayed to the wider electricity-consuming public as a burden on the national grid and electricity tariffs.

The reality, in my assessment, is quite the opposite. Rooftop solar has helped reduce electricity generation costs while strengthening the country's energy independence.

This contribution benefits Sri Lanka's approximately 7.9 million electricity consumers, not merely those who have installed solar panels.

2. Rooftop solar is a people's investment, not a privilege for large businesses

Feed-in tariffs are applicable to renewable energy projects below 10 MW. However, when we examine the installed capacity under this framework, the average project size is reportedly less than 50 kW.

This tells us something extremely important.

The success of distributed solar generation in Sri Lanka has largely been driven by ordinary citizens, households, small businesses and commercial establishments rather than large-scale corporate investors.

These investments have enabled Sri Lankans to participate directly in electricity generation, with the associated economic benefits distributed among thousands of households and businesses.

The financial returns remain within the wider community rather than being concentrated among a handful of large corporations.

This is one of the most significant economic and social achievements of Sri Lanka's rooftop solar program.

3. Feed-in tariffs and competitive tenders must coexist

Many countries successfully adopt a combination of feed-in tariffs for smaller renewable energy installations and competitive tendering for larger projects.

There is a sound reason for this approach.

While competitive tenders can be effective for large-scale procurement, they also involve considerable complexities, including land acquisition, financing, regulatory approvals, grid connectivity, contractual negotiations and project execution risks.

Sri Lanka's own experience demonstrates why a balanced approach is necessary.

Consider the 100 MW Siyambalanduwa solar project.

While rooftop solar installations are generally compensated at approximately Rs. 17 per unit or less, the Siyambalanduwa tender was reportedly awarded at approximately US$0.08 per unit, equivalent to around Rs. 28 at the exchange rate used in this comparison.

Furthermore, a US dollar-linked tariff exposes the cost of electricity to exchange-rate fluctuations, potentially increasing the rupee-denominated cost if our currency depreciates.

Despite the project having been awarded approximately three years ago, it has reportedly yet to deliver electricity to the national grid.

Meanwhile, thousands of rooftop solar investors have already completed their installations and are generating electricity.

This is the fundamental difference between announcing generation capacity and actually delivering electricity to consumers.

4. Who really delivered the additional 1,500 MW?

There has been a claim that approximately 1,500 MW of solar capacity was added during the past two years.

However, we must ask a fundamental question: who actually invested in and developed this capacity?

The overwhelming contribution has come from Sri Lankan prosumers — electricity consumers who have invested their own capital to generate electricity and supply surplus energy to the grid.

Approximately 160,000 rooftop solar installations are reportedly connected to the national network.

These investments were not directly financed or constructed by the Government. They were undertaken by households, entrepreneurs and businesses responding to the opportunities created by the existing renewable energy framework.

The Government's role in facilitating this investment is important, but the investment itself belongs to the people.

There also appears to be a discrepancy in the figures presented for capacity additions during 2024–2026, including a reference to 1,040 kW. These figures require clarification and reconciliation with official installation statistics.

5. The promise of another 2,600 MW by next year

We are now being told that an additional 2,600 MW of solar generation capacity will be developed by next year.

I seriously question the feasibility of this projection.

Large-scale renewable energy projects require substantial time for financing, land acquisition, environmental clearances, grid connection approvals, procurement and construction.

Announcing ambitious capacity targets is relatively easy. Delivering operational power plants is an entirely different matter.

The real measure of success is not how many megawatts are announced, tendered or awarded, but how many megawatts are actually commissioned and supplying electricity to the grid.

I would welcome being proven wrong, but I remain deeply sceptical that the announced capacity will materialise within the stated timeframe.

I am also concerned about the allocation process relating to approximately 650 MW of proposed projects. I have initiated legal proceedings concerning these matters, and the relevant issues are therefore subject to judicial consideration.

Transparency, fairness and compliance with the applicable legal framework must remain fundamental to renewable energy procurement.

6. Floating solar: Major opportunity being overlooked

Floating solar offers Sri Lanka a significant opportunity to expand renewable electricity generation without competing extensively for valuable land.

The proposed 5 MW Bankatuwa floating solar project, for example, has been identified as a feed-in tariff project rather than a competitively tendered project.

More importantly, proposals have been made to develop large-scale floating solar and battery storage facilities in the Puttalam Lagoon area.

One such concept envisages covering approximately 13% of the lagoon with solar installations, supported by battery storage, as a potential alternative to conventional thermal generation at Norochcholai.

If technically, environmentally and economically feasible, such an initiative could significantly reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, strengthen national energy security and contribute towards Sri Lanka's net-zero ambitions.

There is also the broader possibility of utilising portions of major reservoirs for floating solar installations.

Preliminary proposals have suggested that covering approximately 15% of suitable reservoir surfaces could provide substantial electricity generation capacity, potentially enough to meet a significant share of national requirements.

Such concepts require rigorous feasibility studies, environmental assessments and implementation planning. Nevertheless, they deserve serious consideration rather than being overlooked.

7. Grid curtailment: Why are we restricting solar instead of fixing the network?

The discussion on renewable energy storage brings us to perhaps the most important issue.

Sri Lanka is increasingly curtailing solar generation, but where is the transparent, transformer-by-transformer technical assessment identifying the actual constraints?

There are reportedly more than 33,000 distribution transformers across the national electricity network.

According to information available to me, fewer than 500 transformers may be experiencing significant technical difficulties associated with high daytime solar penetration.

If these figures are confirmed, the affected transformers would represent approximately 1.5% of the total transformer population.

Yet the response appears to be broad curtailment rather than identifying and resolving the specific technical problems.

To my knowledge, no comprehensive, publicly available assessment has been presented demonstrating that widespread restrictions are the most appropriate solution.

A proper engineering study should identify the affected transformers and feeders, establish their hosting capacities and determine the most cost-effective remedies.

These could include network reinforcement, improved voltage regulation, modern inverter controls, transformer upgrades and appropriately located battery storage.

Where justified, installing Battery Energy Storage Systems at affected distribution transformers or upstream network locations could absorb surplus daytime solar electricity and release it during the evening peak.

Even a carefully designed, limited curtailment regime — potentially around 15% at identified constraint points, if supported by technical studies — could prove considerably less disruptive than blanket restrictions.

We should identify the problem, measure it and solve it — not penalise the entire renewable energy sector for constraints that may be concentrated in a small portion of the network.

8. Battery storage incentives must be available to everyone

I personally submitted proposals requesting that renewable energy battery storage systems be made available duty-free.

The objective was straightforward: make storage affordable for households, small businesses and distributed renewable energy investors, thereby reducing pressure on the grid and encouraging greater self-consumption.

Unfortunately, the benefits introduced appear to have been directed primarily towards larger-scale investors.

If we genuinely want distributed battery storage to support grid stability, the policy framework must also encourage smaller installations.

Energy storage should not become an opportunity reserved for large businesses while ordinary consumers are excluded from the benefits.

9. The hidden cost of thermal generation

We also hear claims about reducing or eliminating diesel-based electricity generation.

However, consumers continue to bear the cost of thermal generation capacity through contractual capacity payments, even when certain plants generate little or no electricity.

Based on the capacity payment estimates I have referred to, consumers effectively bear an additional cost equivalent to approximately Rs. 2 per unit of electricity consumption.

A further combined-cycle power plant under development could potentially increase this burden by an estimated Rs. 1 per unit.

These figures require confirmation against the relevant power purchase agreements and national electricity sales data, but the underlying issue is important.

Capacity payments can remain payable even when generation is low, and US dollar-linked contractual obligations can expose the electricity system to exchange-rate risk.

There are also serious questions regarding the utilisation of existing thermal generation capacity.

According to the operating figures available to me, one 300 MW unit recorded a plant factor of approximately 40% last year, while another reportedly operated for less than one week in total.

These figures warrant independent verification, but they highlight why generation planning must examine actual utilisation, contractual obligations and the full cost borne by consumers.

10. We must not undermine the very sector that has delivered results

Sri Lanka has built approximately 3,000 MW of solar generation capacity, of which around 2,550 MW is reportedly associated with rooftop installations.

This achievement was made possible largely through investments by Sri Lankan citizens and businesses.

At a time when the country needs affordable electricity, energy independence, foreign exchange savings and greater renewable energy penetration, we should be strengthening this successful model.

Instead, proposals to remove established rooftop solar mechanisms and alter investment conditions risk undermining the confidence of those who have already invested and discouraging future participation.

We cannot expect citizens to invest their savings under one set of rules and then change the goalposts midway through the match.

The appropriate response to increasing renewable energy penetration is to modernise the grid, improve system planning, introduce storage and develop transparent, technically justified operating procedures.

Sri Lanka should not dismantle a successful distributed renewable energy model simply because its electricity infrastructure and operational practices have failed to evolve at the same pace.

If we undermine the rooftop solar sector without delivering viable alternatives, we risk moving from a difficult situation into an even worse one.

That would be a serious setback for affordable electricity, national energy security and the country's renewable energy future.

title: Government must heed cry for fairer taxes and quell storm | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 16 October 2026 00:23
-     - 66

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake

The streets of Colombo are echoing with the cries of the working class agitating for fairer taxes. The Jana Aragala Movement and the Frontline Socialist Party staged a protest march in Colombo on 3 October, demanding the removal of unfair tax policies and relief from the rising cost of living. 

The National Power (NPP) Government must not treat this as just a minor political disturbance. It must treat it as the desperate gasp of ordinary people for economic survival. Ordinary men and women of Sri Lanka are hurting from the impacts of a double-edged sword. On one side is a direct taxation formula that has scant respect for the modest earnings of professionals and workers who keep the nation's engine running. On the other side is the jagged edge of indirect taxes such as value-added taxes (VAT) that tax the flour in a mother’s kitchen, the books in a child’s bag, and the medicine on a pensioner’s table with total disregard for the ability of the individual to pay. The NPP was swept into office on the solemn promise of justice, equity, and relief for a weary populace. Tom, Dick and Harry have been patient. They want Sri Lanka to prosper. Yet, when the state unceasingly balances its ledgers on the broken backs of the poor, this social contract will fracture. The subject protest is a stark reminder that true economic recovery cannot be built on the slow starvation of the common man. Whilst I applaud the key achievements of the NPP, I believe that it is time for it to re-examine the human cost of its tax arithmetic. There is a need to quell the storm before it becomes a cyclone.

The challenges faced by the NPP in maintaining fiscal discipline to satisfy international obligations are enormous. However, ignoring tax relief for ordinary citizens carries severe risks. The NPP’s victory was powered by the working and middle classes. Hardships emanating from persistent tax pressures risk alienating this core base, breeding cynicism and public disillusionment. When applied indiscriminately, regressive indirect taxes severely curb disposable income, stifle domestic consumption, lower savings capacity, drag down small business growth, and impede national recovery. Unaddressed cost-of-living grievances also threaten political and social stability, risking street protests and labour strikes that can severely damage investor confidence. Furthermore, high direct income tax burdens on skilled professionals and technical experts accelerate a devastating brain drain that erodes national capacity. Delivering targeted tax relief is therefore not merely a social gesture, but it is a political and economic imperative for the long-term prosperity of Sri Lanka.

Opinions may differ, but the facts are stubborn in noting that, in its first two years, the NPP Government has achieved substantial progress in stabilising a fragile nation. There were skeptics who thought that the new Government would crumble within a year. But, in truth, it has successfully halted economic collapse, avoided hyperinflation, brought transparency to state spending, and dismantled long-standing political privileges and systemic corruption. By expanding targeted social safety nets and maintaining fiscal discipline, the administration has demonstrated the political maturity required to steady the economy and rebuild international credibility. However, macro-level stability remains incomplete if it fails to translate into micro-level relief for ordinary citizens. The current cost of living crisis is the painful, inevitable residue of decades when Sri Lanka systematically lived beyond its means, relying on unsustainable debt, consuming unearned wealth, and enjoying meaningless subsidies. The necessary structural adjustments, fiscal consolidation, and currency corrections have been largely taken and/or are being taken. Great!

With the economy now reset on a firmer baseline, there must be a fundamental shift in the strategy for revenue generation. For years, the state has relied disproportionately on regressive indirect taxes, such as VAT, which unfairly burden low- and middle-income families because they are applied uniformly to essentials regardless of the earning capacity of the subjected individuals. Therefore, to make relief sustainable, the NPP must aggressively shift the tax composition toward direct taxation by widening the direct tax net, rationalising non-strategic tax concessions and ensuring that high earners pay their fair share.

Broadening the national taxpayer base is a fundamental structural necessity for achieving long-term fiscal stability, economic resilience, and social fairness. Extracting additional revenue from a narrow pool of compliant taxpayers depresses private investment, encourages capital flight, and drives economic activity into the informal domain. Transitioning to a broad-based, lower-rate tax environment requires a systematic sequence of actions including digital integration, administrative modernisation, targeted enforcement, and low-friction identification frameworks. The actions must move beyond simply issuing mandatory Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TINs) and pivot toward data-driven enforcement. By integrating the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) with key Government departments, customs, financial institutions, land registries, and motor traffic databases, the state can map wealth against declared incomes. Automated cross-referencing of high-value transactions, such as luxury vehicle purchases, primary real estate transfers, and offshore credit card spending, can allow the more effective identification of undisclosed wealth. 

Additionally, better coverage of high-income earners can be achieved if professional bodies covering medical, legal, engineering, and accounting fields can be requested to condition annual practicing license renewals on active tax registration and compliant filing status. After all, a professional’s primary allegiance is to the public! So what is the problem?


Bringing micro, small, and medium enterprises as well as independent self-employed professionals into the formal economy requires eliminating administrative complexity. Complex filing requirements, obscure regulations, and fear of arbitrary assessment drive small business owners into unrecorded cash operations. To lower this barrier, tax authorities must introduce simplified compliance regimes featuring user-friendly, mobile-based filing applications, transparent turnover declarations, and flat-rate tax options. Lengthy, jargon-heavy return forms discourage voluntary participation, especially among first-time taxpayers and micro-enterprises. Returns should be condensed into plain-language digital documents that citizens can complete confidently without hiring expensive consultants. Digital transactions, as opposed to cash transactions, must be encouraged through incentives or by regulation. Expanding the direct tax base in this way will boost state revenue, reduce the dependency on indirect tax, and foster public trust in fiscal equity. Bringing unregistered wealth into the formal net is challenging but not impossible. If there is a will, there is always a way! The NPP Government has the will.

The rapid expansion of cross-border e-commerce, digital entertainment, ride-hailing platforms, and freelance digital work has created substantial revenue potential that remains largely uncaptured by traditional tax rules. Establishing simplified digital registration portals and platform-based withholding mechanisms will allow the state to capture consumption and vendor taxes at the source without imposing heavy administrative burdens on individual gig workers. Concurrently, specialised audit teams equipped with forensic accounting capabilities can be established to review complex corporate structures, multi-layered trusts, and offshore assets. Fully leveraging international tax transparency frameworks, such as automatic exchange of information networks, can also ensure better monitoring of offshore accounts and foreign holdings.

Administrative reform

Executing a successful taxpayer expansion plan requires managing administrative capacity and public perception. Expanding enforcement during periods of high living costs can trigger public resistance if citizens feel overburdened without seeing improvements in public services. Public communication must frame tax enforcement around equity and shared responsibility, demonstrating that expanding the base protects vulnerable populations and creates space to lower direct tax rates on formal wage earners in the future. The IRD can also include automated risk-scoring algorithms within its core software systems to quickly identify significant revenue gaps, enabling staff to focus on substantial tax discrepancies rather than on petty, low-value issues. It must be a policy of management by exception.  Digital innovation must drive this transition. 

Expanding the national tax base also requires an attitudinal change in the IRD. It must shift from a punitive personality to a customer-centric service personality grounded in empathy, soft skills, and administrative simplification. For decades, the relationship between the IRD and the public has been defined by friction, distrust, and confrontation. Taxpayers view the administration as an adversarial body focused on penalties and audits rather than public service. Unregistered citizens and small business owners avoid entering the tax net out of fear that registration will expose them to arbitrary assessments and hostile scrutiny. Reframing the IRD requires developing social soft skills across its workforce. Frontline tax officers and auditors must undergo training in clear communication, dispute de-escalation, and conflict resolution. Taxpayer interactions should feel like collaborative consultations rather than interrogations, guiding citizens toward corrective action rather than issuing immediate penalty notices. Establishing a supportive tone will demystify tax administration and transform compliance from legal coercion into a shared social responsibility. 

Reforming tax dispute resolution is equally vital. The IRD must distinguish between honest mistakes and deliberate fraud by offering fast-track review mechanisms, mediation, and penalty-waiver programs for voluntary self-correction. Finally, transparent public education campaigns must frame taxation as a mutual civic commitment funding healthcare, education, transportation, and infrastructure. Changing the IRD’s culture to embrace empathy and accessibility is vital in rebuilding public trust and sustainably broadening Sri Lanka’s taxpayer base.

Tax adjustments

Economic stabilisation under the IMF program has restored macroeconomic stability, but at a severe cost to middle-class professionals and fixed-income earners. The current statutory personal income tax threshold is woefully inadequate, as costs of basics like food, utilities, transport, and healthcare immediately absorb household earnings. Furthermore, narrow tax bands starting at low-income levels push ordinary workers quickly into top-tier brackets, eroding savings, dampening consumer spending, and inducing a brain drain of skilled talent. To deliver tangible relief, the Government must implement a multi-pronged adjustment to the direct tax structure. 

First, raising the tax-free threshold and widening lower tax brackets would align taxation with post-inflation living costs, preventing middle-income earners from losing over a third of their marginal income. Second, introducing targeted tax deductions for essential outlays such as education, health insurance, and renewable energy would directly ease financial pressure on working families while incentivising formal economic activity and social investment. Achieving this domestic tax relief without destroying fiscal targets and fiscal discipline is fraught with challenges and requires careful, holistic thought. There will be winners and losers.

Ending the regime of arbitrary corporate tax exemptions for projects, irrespective of their strategic importance, is one that fits directly into this thinking. By ensuring that large foreign and domestic corporations contribute their fair share to the treasury, the state can build the fiscal space necessary to lighten the tax burden on its working population. Tax concessions granted under frameworks like the Strategic Development Projects (SDP) Act were intended to attract transformative, high-technology foreign direct investment (FDI) that yields spillovers in industrial capacity, technology transfer, and job creation. 

Global evidence demonstrates that serious, high-value investors prioritise structural factors such as transparent legal systems, policy consistency, efficient logistics, streamlined contract enforcement, and a skilled workforce, far above fiscal incentives. However, ill-thought-out tax concessions have frequently diverted vital public revenue into speculative or low-yield sectors. 

A prime example is the real estate and luxury apartment sector. Granting SDP status, along with decade-long corporate tax holidays and import duty waivers on construction materials, to luxury residential developments misaligns with core national priorities. Luxury apartments predominantly serve high-net-worth capital preservation and yield speculative returns rather than driving export-led growth or high-skilled industrial employment. When luxury real estate projects receive blanket tax exemptions, the state effectively forfeits billions in potential revenue from a sector that relies heavily on public infrastructure, municipal services, and domestic land resources. The NPP must introduce strict, deliberate criteria for granting strategic concessions. Tax incentives should be reserved strictly for pioneering manufacturing, green technology, export-oriented and foreign exchange-earning ventures, and critical supply-chain infrastructure. Consumer real estate and luxury residential projects should be explicitly excluded from strategic status. Ending these unnecessary tax holidays ensures that high-value commercial ventures contribute their fair share to the treasury, relieving pressure to tax ordinary citizens.

The Government should also tap another readily available revenue source. Under current fiscal policy, gains from Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) shares are fully exempt from Capital Gains Tax (CGT), while land, private shares, and real estate are taxed. Though intended to boost liquidity and portfolio investment, this exemption creates a stark imbalance. Wealthy investors realise millions tax-free while working families pay high VAT on essential goods. It may also divert savings from productive investment. To address this disparity without undermining liquidity, the Government could replace the blanket exemption with a modest 5–10% CGT rate or adopt a structure exempting gains if a share has been held for a minimum period. Such a low-friction tax would generate stable revenue from accumulated financial wealth and signal a commitment to progressive taxation by ensuring financial capital contributes alongside labour income.

It is time for the Government to reward the patience of the ordinary citizens. This must be done without delay. To build a resilient economic foundation, the Government must urgently widen its domestic tax base to distribute the fiscal burden equitably across society. Broadening the tax net is essential to protecting the purchasing power of ordinary citizens who form the backbone of the economy. Revenue generation must be founded on systemic fairness. The system must not browbeat the compliant and overtax the vulnerable. In tandem with this domestic shift, foreign direct investment should be actively pursued but strictly guided toward strategic national priorities through a transparent, infrastructure-led model rather than wasteful, untargeted tax concessions. Bringing capital gains on listed shares into the tax base can further reinforce fiscal equity by requiring financial wealth generation to contribute fairly. By making a broader, more inclusive tax base the pillar of domestic policy, alongside targeted foreign capital inflows and capital gains taxation, Sri Lanka can establish a sustainable economic model that drives long-term growth while safeguarding social welfare.

title: Key income tax deadlines before December ends | Daily FT
summary:

Between now and end December 2026, Sri Lankan taxpayers will be closing one tax year while funding the next. Y/A 2025/26 ended on 31 March 2026, and the return of income must be filed by 30 November 2026. Instalments for Y/A 2026/27 now operate on a new basis under the Inland Revenue (Amendment) Act, No. 11 of 2026, with the second instalment due on or before 15 November 2026. The two years of assessment are linked, so an error in one can flow into the other.

Key dates at a glance

The table below sets out the dates that matter between now and the end of the year in relation to income tax, APIT, AIT/WHT, transfer pricing and Country by Country (CbC) notification/reporting.

Withholding Tax: Monthly deadlines

AIT/WHT and APIT deducted in a month must be remitted to the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) by the 15th of the following month. Accordingly, deductions made in September, October and November are due on 15 October, 15 November and 15 December, respectively.

The scope of withholding has also widened. From 3 June 2026, the 5% WHT on service fees paid to resident individuals exceeding Rs. 100,000 per month applies to a broader group of professionals. Where a business makes such a payment, 5% must be deducted and remitted to the IRD. The recipient may claim the corresponding credit in the return of income based on the WHT certificate. The expanded group includes auditors, valuers, coaches, personal trainers, artists, actors, musicians, photographers, videographers, therapists, counsellors, beauticians, electricians, dentists, veterinarians, event organisers, social media specialists, brand ambassadors, IT specialists, advertising agents, advisers, translators, writers and debt collectors. The Commissioner General may prescribe additional categories.

Four other withholding changes in the Amendment Act deserve a place on the payer’s checklist:

Payers who have not updated their vendor lists may be under-withholding without realising it. Recipients should, in turn, reconcile their tax credits with the relevant certificates, as unsupported or unverified credits may lead to assessments.

Quarterly instalments 2026/27

All instalment deadlines for Y/A 2025/26 have passed, while the second instalment for Y/A 2026/27 falls due on 15 November 2026.

The Statement of Estimated Tax (SET) has been abolished and does not apply to Y/A 2026/27. Under Section 90(3), each instalment is now calculated by reference to the preceding year’s taxable income using a single formula.

The instalment formula: (A – C) ÷ B

A is the tax on the previous year’s taxable income (here, 2025/26), before deducting any credit.

B is the number of instalments remaining, including the current one (4, 3, 2 and 1).

C is the tax already paid or credited before the due date, including earlier instalments and WHT/AIT.

The IRD’s Circular No. SEC/2026/E/06 (Re-Revised), dated 12 August 2026, explains how “A” is determined. It provides three methods, and the choice is not a matter of convenience.

Method 1 is the default. A taxpayer who is eligible for it cannot use the alternatives. Method 2 covers four situations:

(i) no taxable income last year and none expected, where “A” is zero;

(ii) no taxable income last year but income expected as losses or exemptions end;

(iii) a significant fall in income expected this year; and

(iv) newly registered taxpayers.

Method 3 serves as a safety valve in unusual circumstances.

Three practical points follow from the circular:

The estimate must then be revised for the second quarterly instalment based on the actual tax return for Y/A 2025/26, and the prescribed declarations must be submitted to the Department. Only one revision is permitted.

The second instalment falls due on Sunday, 15 November. Payment should therefore reach the IRD by Friday, 13 November, or, where payment is made online, by 15 November. A shortfall attracts interest and, if it remains unpaid 14 days after the due date, a 10% penalty. Taxpayers should therefore quantify and settle any catch-up amount before the deadline.

30 November: Return and supporting documents

The Return of Income for Y/A 2025/26 must be filed on or before 30 November 2026. As the final tax liability for Y/A 2025/26 affects the instalment computation for Y/A 2026/27, it is important to finalise that liability before determining the second quarter instalment for Y/A 2026/27.

For a company, the filing package typically includes the following documents, with the TPDF submitted together with the Return of Income where applicable:

A return lodged without audited accounts is treated as not furnished. Taxpayers who need more time can write to the Commissioner General under Section 130 before 30 November, but this does not extend the payment date.

The same deadline, 30 November, applies to the Y/A 2026/27 instalment documentation, which may be uploaded to RAMIS together with the return for Y/A 2025/26:

This should be submitted by taxpayers who used Method 2 for the first quarter, together with supporting calculations. Attachment 1 (Revised) should be filed where the estimate changes.

This should be submitted by newly registered taxpayers estimating their income for the current year.

Taxpayers claiming tax credits when calculating their quarterly income tax liability are also required to submit the prescribed Statement of Tax Credit Schedule under Notice No. SEC/PN/IT/2026-05. The schedule must be furnished to the IRD by 30 November 2026. Where the tax credit position changes during the year, a separate schedule must be submitted for the relevant instalment. If the credits remain unchanged, the first-quarter schedule remains valid for the entire year.

2 December: Interest-relief deadline

Section 42 of the Amendment Act discharges interest on late payments and underpayments of income tax, including withholding taxes, the Surcharge Tax and the Debt Repayment Levy. It covers assessments up to Y/A 2024/25. The condition is that the full principal tax is paid by 2 December 2026. Penalties may be waived on written requests showing reasonable cause, and any penalty still payable must also be settled by that date. Taxpayers with pending audits, reviews or appeals can settle and still qualify. 

Taxpayers carrying old arrears should treat 2 December as a firm deadline and an opportunity to settle outstanding principal tax and obtain the available interest relief.

31 December: Country-by-Country reporting

Transfer pricing obligations also extend beyond the 30 November return-filing deadline. Constituent entities of qualifying multinational enterprise groups should ensure that the prescribed Country-by-Country (CbC) reporting notification for Y/A 2025/26 is submitted by 31 December 2026, where applicable. This notification requirement should be considered by both March and December year-end entities.

In addition, a qualifying reporting entity with a reporting fiscal year ended 31 December 2025 must submit its CbC Report by 31 December 2026, being within 12 months of the end of that reporting fiscal year. Taxpayers should distinguish between the notification obligation, which identifies the reporting entity, and the separate obligation to file the CbC Report itself.

Compliance pressure and the case for simplification

Taxpayers should not underestimate the consequences of non-compliance. Interest on unpaid tax continues to accrue at 1.5% per month from the original due date, while a penalty of 20% may apply where tax remains unpaid 14 days after the due date. For unpaid quarterly instalments, a 10% penalty may apply.

The coming months will be particularly significant for taxpayers, with several key income tax filing and payment obligations falling within a relatively short period. Unlike in previous years, taxpayers must navigate a range of new requirements, many of which converge in November. Given the potential exposure to interest and penalties, taxpayers should clarify their obligations and address the relevant compliance requirements well before the deadlines.

At the same time, the growing number of forms, schedules and reporting obligations highlights the need for continued simplification of Sri Lanka’s tax compliance framework. While taxpayers must meet their obligations, policymakers and tax administrators should remain focused on reducing complexity and making it easier to calculate, report and pay tax. A tax system that is simple, predictable and user-friendly not only supports voluntary compliance but also strengthens Sri Lanka’s ease of doing business and overall investment climate. The above reflects only the key deadlines stemming from the Inland Revenue Act. Compliance dates under other tax laws such as Value Added Tax (VAT) and Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL) are separate and are not covered in this article, so taxpayers should ensure these are tracked as well.
