Introduction

Essential oils are highly concentrated volatile compounds extracted from aromatic plants and have been used for centuries in medicine, food preservation, cosmetics, perfumery, and cultural practices. In recent decades, global demand for natural ingredients has accelerated due to growing consumer awareness regarding health, sustainability, and environmentally responsible products. Consequently, the essential oil industry has evolved into a significant contributor to the global bioeconomy, supporting pharmaceuticals, food and beverages, cosmetics, personal care, household products and aromatherapy.

Sri Lanka possesses unique advantages within this expanding global market. As one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, the country harbours remarkable floral diversity, diverse climatic zones and centuries of traditional knowledge. This review evaluates the current status of Sri Lanka's essential oil industry, identifies technological and market opportunities, assesses existing constraints, and proposes strategic directions for sustainable industrial growth.

Historical evolution of Sri Lanka's essential oil industry

Sri Lanka's association with aromatic plants extends back more than two millennia. Situated on the Maritime Silk Road, the island became renowned for premium spices, particularly true Ceylon cinnamon. Colonial administrations expanded commercial spice cultivation but emphasised export of raw commodities with limited local value addition. Following independence, cultivation diversified into pepper, citronella, clove, nutmeg, ginger, turmeric, vanilla and medicinal plants. Today, traditional knowledge combined with scientific innovation offers considerable opportunities for producing premium essential oils for international markets. In recently published National Export Development Plan (NEDP) 2026-2030 by Export Development Board (EDB), Spices and concentrates business domain is identified as a priority sector.

Sri Lanka's position in the global essential oil market

Global demand for essential oils continues to grow due to increasing use in fragrances, flavours, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and nutraceuticals. Sri Lanka contributes only a small proportion of global exports despite its comparative advantages. Currently Sri Lanka holds the 31st position in global essential oil exports and serves 0.5% of the global demand. Principal export markets include the United States, India, Germany, Spain, France, the United Kingdom, Canada, China and Australia. Cinnamon leaf oil and cinnamon bark oil remain the flagship export products owing to the unique quality of Ceylon cinnamon. Growing consumer demand for natural and sustainably sourced ingredients provides significant opportunities for expanding Sri Lanka's global market share through value addition and branding.

India is a major export destination for Sri Lanka. Exports to India in year 2024.

Production systems, resource base and major essential oil crops

Sri Lanka's favourable climate supports numerous aromatic crops including cinnamon, pepper, citronella, clove, nutmeg, ginger, turmeric, cardamom and vanilla. Production is dominated by smallholder farmers operating diversified farming systems. Cinnamon remains the flagship crop with production concentrated in Galle, Matara, Kalutara and Ratnapura. Conventional steam distillation remains the dominant extraction method. Modernisation of processing infrastructure and industrial-scale value addition are needed to improve competitiveness and export earnings.

Quality assurance and regulatory framework

Quality assurance underpins international competitiveness. Exporters increasingly comply with ISO standards, GMP, HACCP and organic certification requirements. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) is the principal analytical technique used to verify authenticity and chemical composition. Institutions including the Industrial Technology Institute, Sri Lanka Standards Institution and National Plant Quarantine Service support quality control and certification. Expanding laboratory access and certification among small producers remains a priority.

Technological innovations transforming Sri Lanka's essential oil industry

Emerging technologies such as supercritical CO₂ extraction, molecular fractionation and blockchain traceability are reshaping the industry. Artificial intelligence, precision agriculture and IoT technologies offer opportunities to optimise harvesting, improve extraction efficiency and strengthen quality assurance. Strategic investment in innovation will enable Sri Lanka to transition from crude oil exports towards high-value fragrance and flavour ingredients.

Recent research and development

Recent research has highlighted the antimicrobial, antioxidant and therapeutic properties of Sri Lankan essential oils, particularly Ceylon cinnamon, black pepper, clove, nutmeg and citronella. Advances in extraction optimisation, phytochemical characterisation and formulation technologies continue to expand applications in food preservation, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and nutraceuticals. Increased collaboration among

universities, research institutes and industry will accelerate commercialisation of novel products.

Challenges and future directions

The industry faces challenges including fragmented production, inconsistent quality, inadequate industrial processing, limited research investment and climate change. Nevertheless, rising global demand for sustainable natural products creates significant opportunities. Investment in industrial distillation, aroma chemicals, specialty ingredients, traceability systems, climate-resilient agriculture and international branding will strengthen Sri Lanka's competitiveness. Also, Sri Lanka can be a hub for Flavours and Fragrances industry. Recently few global multinationals established research and development centers in Dubai and Singapore. Due to the geographic location Sri Lanka could be one of the best locations for a research center.

Conclusions

Sri Lanka possesses exceptional biodiversity, a globally recognised spice heritage and favourable agro-climatic conditions that position it to become a leading supplier of premium essential oils. Technological innovation, quality assurance, research investment and strategic policy support are essential for moving beyond commodity exports towards high-value fragrance, flavour and wellness products. Coordinated action among Government, academia and industry can transform the essential oil sector into a major contributor to sustainable economic development.

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

Sri Lanka are facing one of their most daunting periods in international cricket where for the next four months their capabilities as a white ball nation will be tested to the hilt as they play all their matches abroad.

Sri Lanka’s struggles in international cricket, particularly in limited-overs formats (T20I), have been going on for well over a decade. While they have always struggled away from home, things improved somewhat on home soil after 2021. So, whenever they returned from a disappointing overseas tour, there was usually a home series to help them regroup, rebuild confidence, and ease the pressure.

But that breathing space is now no longer available.

Since the last T20 World Cup ended in March 2026, Sri Lanka have been caught in an inexorable cycle of away tours. It started in the Caribbean where they lost the T20I series 2-1, continued in England where they were whitewashed 3-0, and has now taken them to Pakistan where they were beaten 2-1. India is next in December where they play three T20Is, followed by New Zealand in January for another three-match T20I series.

Sri Lanka’s only home assignment during this period was the two-Test series against India in August which they lost 1-0 (1 drawn). They won’t return home for another series until the Tests against South Africa in February.

For over a decade, one of Sri Lanka’s biggest weaknesses has been playing away from home. And now, they have to confront that very weakness tour after tour, without even the slightest opportunity to hide anywhere. With two of the toughest assignments, India and New Zealand yet to come, you could still expect the worst.

When compared to countries like India and West Indies where a parallel T20I series is taking place, Sri Lanka seems to be far behind in the game. Their cricket has not evolved the way T20 cricket has since it first came on the scene internationally in 2005. While other countries have been able to adapt to the changes the game is undergoing, Sri Lanka have lost track of what needs to be done to be on par with the others.

In today’s context a winning score in T20I cricket is 200 plus, sometimes even that is not enough as the West Indies proved the other day at Ranchi where they chased down 250 and won with nine balls to spare. The last three T20Is in that series have produced a plethora of runs with each team rattling off 200 plus without much sweat.

At the moment Sri Lanka are struggling to get to even 185, and when they are faced with a target in excess of 200 the batting simply collapses, unable to take up the challenge. T20I cricket does not require big hitters who can clear the boundary constantly, but if you are able to keep rotating the strike, you can get to 200 plus quite comfortably. Sri Lanka’s biggest problem is that. By not constantly rotating the strike they build up a lot of dot balls and eventually try to hit their way out of trouble to keep up with the required run rate. This eventually leads to their downfall.

That Sri Lanka was able to avoid another whitewash in Pakistan was because their bowlers were able to keep the home side down to a total of 168, a target which Sri Lanka was capable of chasing down successfully. That alone tells the story of where Sri Lanka’s T20I cricket lies today.

Most of Sri Lanka’s recent coaches had the luxury of playing a reasonable number of home games, providing opportunities to rebuild confidence and ease the pressure after disappointing overseas results. Gary Kirsten and his coaching staff, however, have walked into one of the toughest stretches in recent Sri Lankan cricket history.

Even with all his experience, Kirsten hasn’t been immune to some of the questionable decisions that had plagued previous coaching regimes. Looking at the schedule, things could get even uglier before they get better. And there’s only one way to face this challenge: take it head-on.

There’s no hiding behind home conditions this time. No home advantage to fall back on. Sri Lanka will have to confront their weaknesses in the very conditions where they have struggled for years. It’s a test of strength and character to what the team is capable of. If they can come up trumps it would ease the suffering of thousands of fans who have been yearning to see the day Sri Lanka’s cricket can return to its former glory days.

By Hishan Welmilla

When Galina Basnayake dives into the pool, she carries more than the ambition of an athlete. She carries the hopes of a nation, the rewards of years of dedication and the determination to prove that limitations need not define potential.

One of Sri Lanka’s most promising para swimmers, Galina has steadily established herself on the international stage through outstanding performances in the S9 classification. With multiple international medals, a landmark Asian Para Games achievement and appearances at the highest level of world para swimming, she is building a career that reflects courage, discipline and an unrelenting desire to improve.

Galina’s rise to prominence began with a remarkable performance at the 2021 Asian Youth Para Games in Bahrain, where she captured three gold medals in the women’s 50m, 100m and 400m freestyle events in the S9 category. However, one of the defining moments of her career came at the 4th Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China, in October 2023.

Competing in the women’s 400m freestyle S9 event, Galina produced a superb performance to claim the silver medal in a personal-best time of 5 minutes and 18.28 seconds. Her achievement was particularly significant for Sri Lanka, ending a 13-year wait for a swimming medal at the Asian Para Games.

It was more than a podium finish. It was a breakthrough that reaffirmed Sri Lanka’s potential in international para swimming and placed Galina among the country’s leading athletes in the discipline.

Her performances in Hangzhou demonstrated that she could compete with some of Asia’s best, while providing fresh inspiration to aspiring para athletes across the island.

Galina’s progress has extended beyond regional competition. At the 2024 World Para Swimming Open Water Cup in Sardinia, Italy, she secured a bronze medal in the women’s 3km S7–S10 category, adding another international achievement to her growing collection.

She has also demonstrated her ability to compete beyond the para swimming arena. At the Mount Lavinia Two-mile Sea Swim, she earned recognition as the Best Open Women Para Swimmer, showcasing her endurance and competitive spirit in open-water conditions.

In 2025, Galina continued her international journey at the World Para Swimming Championships in Singapore. Competing against elite swimmers from around the world, she finished ninth in the women’s 400m freestyle S9 event, recording a time of 5:08.47 in the official results.

The result highlighted her continued development and the demanding standards of competition at world championship level.

Behind Galina’s progress is the guidance of renowned Sri Lankan swimmer and coach Julian Bolling, under whose guidance she has trained at Rainbow Aquatics.

Bolling’s experience and technical knowledge have played an important role in helping her develop as a competitive swimmer, while Galina’s commitment to training and willingness to challenge herself continue to drive her progress.

Success in para swimming demands far more than physical ability. It requires technical precision, tactical awareness, endurance, mental strength and the discipline to perform consistently under pressure. Galina’s achievements reflect the importance of these qualities in her journey towards international excellence.

Away from competition, Galina is also pursuing her academic studies in psychology at the Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology (SLIIT).

Balancing university life with the demands of high-performance sport requires careful time management, sacrifice and determination. For Galina, the pursuit of academic knowledge alongside sporting excellence represents another dimension of her ambition.

Her journey offers an important message to young athletes: sporting dreams and educational goals need not be mutually exclusive. With the right support, discipline and commitment, both can become part of a meaningful future.

From three gold medals at the Asian Youth Para Games to silver at the Asian Para Games, a world-level open-water bronze and a top-ten finish at the World Championships, Galina Basnayake has already compiled an impressive record for Sri Lanka.

Yet her story is far from complete.

Every international appearance provides another opportunity to refine her technique, improve her times and gain valuable experience against the world’s best. The challenge now is to build on those achievements, maintain consistency and continue closing the gap on the leading swimmers in her classification.

For Sri Lanka, Galina represents the promise of a new generation of para athletes determined to compete with distinction on the global stage. Her achievements also underline the importance of sustained investment, coaching, facilities and institutional support in helping talented athletes reach their full potential.

In the pool, every second matters. Every stroke demands commitment. And every finish line presents a new challenge.

Galina Basnayake has already shown that she possesses the determination to meet those challenges head-on. As her international journey continues, Sri Lanka will watch with pride and anticipation, hoping that the young para swimmer will add further chapters to a story that has already brought honour to the nation.

For Galina, the medals are milestones, not the destination. The next race is another opportunity to make history.

The warmth of Sri Lankan hospitality gives that service its distinctive character, creating a welcome that feels both intuitive and sincere.

Set among coconut palms overlooking the Indian Ocean, the resort combines the tranquillity of a coastal retreat with opportunities for discovery. At Anantara Spa, Ayurvedic traditions connect guests with the island’s wellness heritage, complemented by experiences that introduce the culture, landscapes and wildlife of southern Sri Lanka.

These recognitions are a proud moment for all of us, and our responsibility is to make that same care evident in every stay.”

Beyond the resort, these achievements add to Sri Lanka’s appeal as a destination for discerning travellers, where a coastal escape can open the door to remarkable culinary, cultural and wellness discoveries. They also underline Tangalle’s place in that story, offering an inviting perspective on the island’s southern shores.

For Anantara Peace Haven Tangalle Resort, this landmark year is both a celebration of its team and an inspiration for the journey ahead. The focus remains on translating recognition into the everyday quality of a stay, giving guests new reasons to discover the resort and returning visitors every reason to feel at home.
